descripcion: At C1 the focus is on adverbs that shift the meaning of the whole sentence depending on their position: only, even, just. Placed differently, the same words emphasise a different part of the sentence entirely — a precision tool, not just a rule to follow.

filas: she didn't fix it, just noticed

ejemplos.texto: Only the manager was informed about the change.
She had only just started when the call came in.
Even the experts couldn't explain it.

notas: Moving only one word changes which part of the sentence is being restricted or emphasised.
Even goes directly before the element it emphasises, whether that's the subject, the verb or the object.
In careful writing, these adverbs are placed precisely; in speech, intonation often does some of the work instead.

contraste.es: El español logra este mismo efecto de énfasis reordenando la oración o usando solo de forma más flexible, sin que la posición cambie tan sistemáticamente el significado. Los hispanohablantes tienden a poner only al principio de la oración por defecto, perdiendo la posibilidad de enfocar una palabra específica en medio de la frase.

errores: Always placing only at the start of the sentence, regardless of what should actually be emphasised.
Misplacing even so it modifies the wrong part of the sentence.
Relying on intonation alone in writing, where position is what actually carries the meaning.
autochequeo: Does the position of only match what I actually want to restrict?
Is even placed directly before the element it emphasises?
Would moving the adverb change the intended meaning?
Have I used position rather than relying only on intonation in writing?
Are at least three different positions of these adverbs used deliberately?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on the position of only, even and just. Check whether each position matches the intended emphasis and flag any sentence where the position seems accidental. Do not rewrite the text.
